For a random kk-regular graph, it is easy to show that the expected average loop size goes to infinity with the number of nodes110, and hence a tree-tensor approach is expected to efficiently perform quantum annealing protocols on such graphs for any finite correlation length. Our kk-regular lattice models, in contrast, have many short loops incident on every site: length 2 for dimerized bicliques, length 4 for dimerized-cubic and square lattices, and length 6 in diamond lattices and non-dimerized 3D lattices. As shown in Section III.2.4, we can use a locally tree-like approximation efficiently in all these lattices for both time updates and estimation of observables—agnostic to the requirement of gauge convergence—but find that for even the shortest experimental time scales and simplest lattices, large systematic errors result.

III.2.4 Simple update

Simple update assumes a locally tree-like approximation for purposes of truncation during time evolution 97. The initial condition of factorized spins meets the locally tree-like gauge conditions. In our annealing context, SU with fine-grained Trotterization ought to track a gauge consistent with BP where such a fixed point is stable109, and so we omit an independent evaluation of BP.

The impact of an unconverged, or converged (but poor), gauge during time evolution is that inferred truncations are uncontrolled. The systematic errors associated with uncontrolled truncation can nevertheless represent a good trade-off when errors in the final state are permissable. SU methods have been successfully applied for the simulation of a kicked Ising model on a heavy-hex lattice for example, which despite finite dimensionality (2) has a paucity of short loops16, 94.

Simple update is based upon an approximation of the bond environment. This environment can be used not only for PEPS truncation in time evolution, but also for estimation of expectation values. We call this approximation SO (simple observable). The self-consistent combination of SO with SU has been successfully applied in related PEPS applications 94, and this method is feasible in all of our lattices.

In application of SU and SO to the experimental regimes many results were well converged, with a weak dependence of ϵc\epsilon_{c} on bond dimension DD (for D≥2D\geq 2). A weak dependence of errors on DD might result from the insufficient neighborhood scale. In some more strongly correlated regimes SU was found to be unstable, with sensitivity to d​tdt and the minimum singular value threshold. This is not unexpected since inversion of small singular values necessary in the algorithm can amplify errors quickly, and locally-tree-like assumptions fail as correlation length grows. We present in Fig. S10 results with d​t={2−7,2−8}​ nsdt=\{2^{-7},2^{-8}\}\,$\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ and D={2,3,4}D=\{2,3,4\} optimized for minimal error on a per instance basis, and with a small (10−1010^{-10}) cutoff in the singular values supported. Correlation error ϵc\epsilon_{c} (NN) is taken only over nearest-neighbor pairs; this quantity correlates strongly with ϵc\epsilon_{c} in (4), but SO environments are local and hence more suited for estimation only of nearest neighbor correlations, so we use the nearest-neighbor variant for convenience. Errors are significantly larger than those obtained from the QPU in our experimental regime (lattices and time scales).

Sources of errors might be attributed to SU or SO. A spin-glass (±J\pm J, low precision) ensemble for small square open-boundary lattices provides a controlled context for this evaluation. SU might be combined with one of: SO; contractions on 2×32{\times}3 neighborhoods (combined with Frobenius norm outside the sublattice, matching the standard NTU update for time-evolution); or exact full contraction. As shown in Fig. S11, SU at small bond dimension combined with SO is accurate for short time scales (ta<1 nst_{a}<$1\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$). 3×23{\times}2 and full contractions improve slightly on errors in these regimes, in line with perturbative loop corrections. SO degrades at longer time scales in a manner that is almost independent of bond dimension, whereas 3×23{\times}2 and full contraction respond to variation in bond dimension, with full contraction superior. For contraction methods, on time scales ≳7 ns\gtrsim$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$, both full and 3×23{\times}2 contractions fail in a manner that cannot be reduced systematically by increasing bond dimension. In this regime the accumulation of errors in SU prevents attainment of small errors by any contraction method for observables. This aligns with our intuition that as correlation length grows more complex, neighborhoods must be contracted 99, 96. We examine this in the context of square and cubic lattices in Sections III.2.6 and III.2.7.

III.2.5 Non-canonical MPS in 1D

In this work we use the standard PEPS techniques that do not refer to canonical forms. Potential advantages of the isometric PEPS 107 seem to be offset by the errors of Moses moves that attempt to change the canonical structure of the network. In order to better understand problems arising from a non-canonical structure of PEPS in 2D, we simulated the Kibble-Zurek (KZ) quench in 1D for an infinite pure-ferromagnetic quantum Ising chain with an infinite MPS ansatz, but without enforcing any canonical gauge. The ansatz is a tensor train with two sublattice tensors: ...−A−B−A−B−…...-A-B-A-B-.... The time evolution is performed in a similar manner as for an infinite PEPS in 2D. Not counting local gates with a transverse field, in each time step there are two 2-site Suzuki-Trotter gates with a ferromagnetic interaction on bonds A​BAB and B​ABA that commute with each other. After the application of a gate, the bond dimension is doubled and has to be truncated back to the original bond dimension DD in a way that minimizes truncation error (see Fig. S12B). The error is measured on a cluster of 2+2​M2+2M sites including the two central sites with the gate and two blocks of MM spins adjacent to the central sites to the left and the right. The error δtig\delta^{g}_{t_{i}} is the Frobenius norm of the relative difference between the clusters before and after the truncation (see Fig. S12B), following application of the gate at time step tit_{i} to a bond g=A​Bg=AB or B​ABA. In the worst-case scenario, the individual errors sum up to a (upper estimate) total truncation error Δg=∑iδtig\Delta_{g}=\sum_{i}\delta^{g}_{t_{i}}. We define the error estimate as

Δ=maxg⁡Δg=max⁡∑ig⁡δtig.\Delta=\max_{g}\Delta_{g}=\max_{g}\sum_{i}\delta^{g}_{t_{i}}. (S4)

For lack of canonical structure, (S4) serves as a rough estimate for a relative error inflicted on observables by the truncations. We will show below that it correlates well with the errors of the expectation values calculated at the end of the quench. Moreover, δtig\delta^{g}_{t_{i}} becomes proportional to d​tdt in the limit of small time steps, making the definition in Eq. (S4), and the quality of the solution, independent of the time-step in that limit. This is illustrated in Fig. S15B in a 2D setup.

The correlation error, Eq. (4) of the main text, after the quench with annealing times 7,14,28 ns7,14,$28\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$, simulated with various cluster sizes MM, is shown in Fig. S13. Overall, a longer annealing time results in a final state with a longer KZ correlation length ξ^∝τQ1/2\hat{\xi}\propto\tau_{Q}^{1/2} and requires a higher bond dimension to reach the same level of accuracyVIVI VI We use ξ^\hat{\xi} to denote the Kibble-Zurek correlation length in line with literature notation. This is to be contrasted with the usage of a more generic correlation length (ξ\xi) elsewhere in our paper (which is not assumed to follow KZ scaling).. Here τQ=ta/t0\tau_{Q}=t_{a}/t_{0} is a dimensionless KZ quench time with t0t_{0} being a characteristic system’s time scale. As we can see in Figure S13, for shortest values of MM the error improves slowly, if at all, with increasing DD. We can also see that for a given DD, the error decreases with the cluster size until it saturates for long enough MM. The minimal MM needed for convergence, McM_{c}, depends on the annealing time. It might be natural to expect Mc∝ξ^∝taM_{c}\propto\hat{\xi}\propto\sqrt{t_{a}}, but it grows faster than ta\sqrt{t_{a}}, as tat_{a}. For example at ta=7 nst_{a}=$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ we can estimate Mc≈16M_{c}\approx 16 while for ta=28 nst_{a}=$28\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ it is four times longer, Mc≈64M_{c}\approx 64. As such, Mc∝taM_{c}\propto t_{a} seems to be more consistent with the data. This steeper scaling is not necessarily at odds with the KZ mechanism. After correlated pairs of quasiparticles with opposite quasimomenta (k,−k)(k,-k) are excited near the critical point, during the following quench across the ferromagnetic phase, they are free to move along the chain and spread their pairwise entanglement. In this way, a second length scale, l=τQ​ln⁡τQl=\sqrt{\tau_{Q}}\ln\tau_{Q}, develops 112 that is longer than ξ^\hat{\xi}. In the limited range of τQ\tau_{Q} where we are operating, what might at first be dismissed as a mere logarithmic correction to ξ^\hat{\xi}, is actually substantial and makes ll appear to grow nearly linearly with τQ∝ta\tau_{Q}\propto t_{a}.

Fig. S13D shows the correlation between the correlation error and the total truncation error in Eq. (S4). The log-log plot is not inconsistent with a linear dependence. It is noteworthy that the correlation error is an order of magnitude lower than the truncation error. We observe that ϵc≈Δ/10\epsilon_{c}\approx\Delta/10 is a good approximation to the data, allowing prediction of the correlation error based on the truncation error.

The 1D toy model shows how important it is for the cluster size to be at least comparable to the range of correlations in order to make efficient use of the limited bond dimension. The issue becomes more important in 2D and 3D where the limitations are more stringent.

III.2.6 2D PEPS

In 2D, we start with the current state-of-the-art algorithm that can match QPU accuracy only for the fastest annealing times considered. We then systematically examine a family of extensions, which reduce errors below QPU level at intermediate time scales (though not for the slowest experimentally relevant quenches). The yastn library implements the various neighborhood contractions discussed in these sections, with example code and further documentation 65.

As our baseline method, we employ the neighborhood tensor update (NTU) 96, 113 with one PEPS tensor assigned to each lattice site. In NTU, the cluster used for truncation includes the two central sites with the gate plus their six nearest neighbor sites, including two loops, as shown in Fig. S12A. Such a neighborhood is contracted numerically-exactly at a cost of 𝒪⁡(D8+p​D7){\cal O}(D^{8}+pD^{7}) operations, where pp is the physical dimension of PEPS tensor. This exactness preserves the desired positivity of the bond metric tensor in Fig. S14A that gets inverted during optimization of the truncation.

We next systematically probe several methods that expand the neighborhood scale considered in the truncation. Within the paradigm of local bond environments that get contracted exactly (preserving positivity), we expand the nearest neighbor (NN) environment in Fig. S14A by adding partial information from the next layer of tensors, treated tree-like (see Fig. S14B). Calculating this metric has the same 𝒪⁡(D8+p​D7){\cal O}(D^{8}+pD^{7}) asymptotic numerical cost. Further extensions involve including extra loops in the exactly-contracted environment, with both next nearest neighbor (NNN) and NNN+ in Fig. S14C,D coming at 𝒪⁡(p​D10){\cal O}(pD^{10}) numerical cost and limiting feasible PEPS bond dimensions to approximately D=8D=8, in practice. Finally, larger environments can be considered, going toward full update. They rely on approximate contraction schemes, such as boundary MPS shown in Fig. S14E. Unlike exact contraction, such approximations do not preserve the non-negativity of the metric tensor.

Another strategy still uses the NTU cluster for truncation, but each PEPS tensor covers a plaquette of 2×22{\times}2 sites, as shown in Fig. S14G. In this way, the NTU cluster of plaquettes covers four times as many qubits as in the standard setup of Fig. S14F. Surprisingly, for many considered protocols, the bond dimension required for the same truncation error is less than a square of the bond dimension in the one-site NTU. Intuitively, two bond indices with dimension DD extending in a given direction out of a 2×22\times 2 plaquette in the one-site PEPS should fuse into one bond index with dimension D2D^{2}. We observe, however, that the dimension needed to achieve equivalent accuracy is lower than D2D^{2}. Such compression is possible because a plaquette represented by a contraction of 4 one-site PEPS tensors is more constrained than the same plaquette covered by a single plaquette tensor (see Fig. S14F and G). This compression also enables a numerically exact contraction of the (four-times bigger) plaquette NTU cluster. This larger effective cluster allows making more efficient use of the truncated bond dimension, contributing to the compression.

In all the above cases, expectation values follow from the approximate contraction of the entire network. We employ a boundary MPS approach adapted to a cylinder. Larger bond dimensions require exploiting Monte Carlo sampling operating in the zz-basis. Here, we follow the approach of Ref. 100, but with a local trial probability distribution. As compared to the deterministic evaluation of correlators, which requires a double-layer PEPS (PEPS contracted with its conjugate), Monte Carlo sampling requires only the contraction of a single (projected) PEPS layer. It is worth noting, that we produce on the order of one MC sample per second for an 8×88\times 8 system at D=10D=10 (running on a single CPU core), which is roughly three orders of magnitude slower than the QPU sampling rate.

We find the systematic errors associated with the calculation of the expectation values to be much smaller than those resulting from approximate truncation in the time evolution part of the simulation. In Fig. S15A, where we collect simulations done for 8×88{\times}8 cylinder lattice, both for high and low inputs precision studied on the QPU, we show the relation between total truncation error in Eq. (S4) and the correlation error ϵc\epsilon_{c}. The latter is roughly an order of magnitude smaller than the corresponding truncation error Δ\Delta among many tested environments for standard and plaquette PEPS and a range of bond dimensions used to simulate time evolution for several annealing times tat_{a}. Interestingly, a rough estimate of the correlation error as Δ/10\Delta/10 is consistent with a similar estimate in the 1D toy example in Fig. S13. This corroborates that time evolution is the main source of errors in the PEPS results and truncation error is a valid metric to estimate the quality of the approximation. We also show in Fig. S15B that the total truncation error becomes roughly independent of the time step in the limit of small time steps. In those simulations, we terminate the dynamics at s=0.6s=0.6. This has insignificant impact on statistics in the case of exact simulation (see Fig. S23A) but prevents PEPS from accumulating extra errors during the last stage of the evolution.

We use the truncation error metric in Fig. S16 to compare the simulation errors with the simulation times, where all times are for the time-evolution only; i.e., without sampling from the final state, executed on a single CPU core. While for ta=2 nst_{a}=$2\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ all tested simulation methods produce errors below QPU precision, already for D=4D=4, longer annealing times require larger environments and bond dimensions. In particular, we identify a plaquette PEPS with NN+ environments as a leading method for 7 ns7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} quenches. However, all tested methods give worse than QPU results for 20 ns20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} quenches. In particular, low-precision inputs prove to be harder to simulate using PEPS (note that the data in Fig. 3 of the main text shows high-precision results). Finally, we note that the simulated problem has a global ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry. We observe that imposing this global symmetry directly in PEPS ansatz does not affect the quality of the results compared to using dense tensors with no symmetry imposed.

III.2.7 3D PEPS

We performed simulations on a cubic L×L×LL{\times}L{\times}L lattice with open boundary conditions and random nearest-neighbor couplings Ji​jJ_{ij} from a uniform distribution in [−1,1][-1,1]. This is a simplification of the dimerized cubic model used in experiments which has twice as many qubits, but the simplification is already challenging enough to highlight limitations in simulation. Five truncation schemes,explained in Fig. S17, were applied. The simplest one is the SVD truncation in A that ignores any tensor environment and requires only 𝒪⁡(p​D7){\cal O}(pD^{7}) operations. Scheme B includes NN tensors but still ignores contractions between them, keeping the numerical cost to calculate the Gramm-Schmidt metric tensor at the same level of 𝒪⁡(p​D7){\cal O}(pD^{7}). Scheme C includes the contractions, raising the cost to 𝒪⁡(D12+p​D11){\cal O}(D^{12}+pD^{11}) operations. Scheme D includes up to third nearest neighbors. In order to keep the cost at the tolerable level of 𝒪⁡(p​D8){\cal O}(pD^{8}) a sequence of SVD truncations to the single leading singular value (SVD1) is applied that renders an approximate tree-like diagram. First the eight double-PEPS tensors at the corners of the diagram are SVD1-truncated and then, after almost all contractions are completed, the four vertical double bonds are cut. Finally, scheme D’ extends D to a 5×5×65\times 5\times 6 cluster with more SVD1 truncations to keep the cost at the same level of 𝒪⁡(p​D8){\cal O}(pD^{8}). As in Section III.2.6 we are able to truncate dynamics at s=0.6s=0.6 with negligible impact on results.

In 2D it was practical to combine neighborhood updates with approximate full contraction, the former being a computational bottleneck. By contrast, the calculation of observables by comparable methods in 3D is a computational bottleneck. The deterministic scheme employing double-layer PEPS 54 is not practical beyond D=4D=4. We also tested code for a 3D generalization of the single-layer Monte Carlo 100, which partly trades the contraction cost for sampling, but it still does not extend much beyond D=4D=4. We estimate that D=6D=6 is the upper limit, if allowed a few months of computations, but DD is expected to grow exponentially with the Kibble-Zurek length and so does the computation cost.

The right panel of Fig. S17 shows the total truncation error as a function of the annealing time for D=4,6D=4,6. For a given bond dimension, the errors of schemes B,C are practically the same, while those of A/D are much larger/smaller, suggesting that the cluster size matters more than the contractions between the nearest-neighbor tensors. For D=4,6D=4,6 the error of scheme D crosses the 2%2\% QPU benchmark around 4 ns4\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}. In the regime of parameters of Fig. S17, the accuracy of the evolution is limited mainly by the cluster size: there is little improvement with increasing DD but much with the size. With approximate contraction, the size could be further increased but, for long-enough annealing time, a crossover to a DD-limited regime would inevitably take place and the cost of time evolution would start to grow exponentially with tat_{a}.

As a means to increase the exactly contractible cluster size, we also attempted a 3D cubic PEPS, similar to the plaquette one in 2D, where a single PEPS tensor covers a cube of 232^{3} sites. In 3D, a one-site PEPS has 4 bond indices with dimension DD extending in each direction out of the 232^{3} cube. In a cube PEPS tensor, the 4 indices can be fused into one index with dimension D4D^{4}. Therefore, the minimum required to simulate the evolution with only the classical nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian (the transverse field set to zero) is D=2D=2 for the one-site PEPS, D2=4D^{2}=4 for the plaquette PEPS, and D4=16D^{4}=16 for the cubic one. The cubic PEPS has a much higher minimal bond dimension than the plaquette one. In 3D, D≥16D\geq 16 may still be feasible for time evolution, despite an overhead due to the physical dimension, 28=2562^{8}=256, but the evaluation of expectation values within a controlled approximation seems out of reach.

IV Measuring the quality of sampled distributions

The computational task we demonstrate is approximately independent and identically distributed sampling from a quenched quantum state projected in the computational basis. The quality of approximation can be captured by various distributional divergence measures: a correlation-error metric ϵc\epsilon_{c} and classical fidelity (ℱ\mathcal{F}, also called Bhattacharyya distance) are presented in the main text.

A popular measure of sampling quality relevant to random-circuit sampling is the cross entropy114; in that application, the target distribution approaches a Porter-Thomas distribution and a cross-entropy-based measure is known to approach 1 from below as a function of gate fidelity. The chaotic nature of the distribution makes spoofing of large values challenging.

In this work, we might define the cross entropy as −⟨log⁡p~​(z)⟩p-\langle\log{\tilde{p}}(z)\rangle_{p}, where p~{\tilde{p}} is the ground-truth probability of states projected in the zz-basis and angled brackets denote an expectation taken by Monte-Carlo sampling of some approximating distribution pp (the QPU). Unfortunately such a measure appears not to be readily bounded in a manner informative for fidelity. Furthermore, and unlike random-circuit distributions, state probabilities in our application are correlated with efficiently calculated statistics (such as ℋP\mathcal{H}_{P}); the strength of correlation with ℋP\mathcal{H}_{P} is controlled monotonically by tat_{a} and noise. It is easy to raise (lower) the cross-entropy measure by preferential sampling of states with low (high) classical energy. Thus the cross-entropy measure is not a useful quality measure.

The interpretation of a cross-entropy measure is made simpler by comparison with (subtraction of) the model entropy, KL​(p,p~)=⟨log⁡p⁡(x)p~⟩p\textit{KL}(p,\tilde{p})=\langle\log\frac{p(x)}{\tilde{p}}\rangle_{p}, yielding a Kullback-Leibler divergence measure that approaches zero only when the distributions are in agreement. The problem with such a measure is twofold: first, it measures the ability of the ground truth to predict model samples; second, the calculation of entropy from sampling requires a number of samples that scales with the model entropy 115, and the estimate can be subject to strong variance if the ground-truth distribution is narrower than the model’s one. To solve the first issue we might consider the opposite form, KL​(p~,p)\textit{KL}({\tilde{p}},p), but the problem of scalability persists with this definition. Due to entropy scaling with system size, we could not formulate an unbiased estimator for either form of KL-divergence that was informative on larger problems. We found that several estimators exhibit related issues, including the classical fidelity. Because the standard techniques for dealing with scaling—coarse graining, binning, and projection of samples into a lower-dimensional space—are challenging to implement without simplifying the computational task, we selected the scalable measure ϵc\epsilon_{c} as our primary metric. As we show, this correlates well with other measures of distribution divergence.

Alongside ϵc\epsilon_{c} we present classical fidelity, ℱ⁡(p,p~)=∑xp⁡(x)​p~​(x)\mathcal{F}(p,\tilde{p})=\sum_{x}\sqrt{p(x){\tilde{p}}(x)}, and total variation distance TV​(p,p~)=12​∑x|p⁡(x)−p~​(x)|\text{TV}(p,\tilde{p})=\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{x}|p(x)-\tilde{p}(x)| as complementary measures to test distribution divergence beyond that captured by two-body correlations. Fidelity is upper bounded by 1 (when distributions agree) and lower bounded by 0; likewise TV is 0 when distributions agree and in (0,1](0,1] otherwise. We present data with 2N2^{N} bins (one per state), but limit usage to smaller scales where the measure is not dominated by sampling bias since, like the entropy-based measures already discussed, the number of samples must scale with entropy to avoid a dominant sampling bias.

Distribution divergence measures, such as ϵc\epsilon_{c} and ℱ\mathcal{F}, compress high-dimensional information to a number. These numbers may be skewed in some non-trivial manner; for example, our measure ϵc\epsilon_{c} is not sensitive to sign-symmetry breaking (p⁡(s)≠p⁡(−s))(p(s)\neq p(-s)). A divergence of this type would yield a strong signal in classical fidelity by contrast. For this reason it is useful to consider several numbers and also contextualize them with additional distributional information where possible. It is also important to demonstrate that our core results, based upon ϵc\epsilon_{c}, are robust to a change in divergence measure. With this in mind, we provide visualizations of the full probability distribution to provide confidence in the measures, and show that if our QPU-equivalent bond-dimension analysis, based on ϵc\epsilon_{c}, is replaced by an analysis based on ℱ\mathcal{F}, no practically significant difference in results is apparent.

Fig. 2C scatters pzp_{z} against p~z\tilde{p}_{z} for 10610^{6} samples drawn from QPU and from approximate MPS at bond dimension χ=64\chi=64. We first extend this data in Fig. S18A, showing the spread of pzp_{z} versus p~z{\tilde{p}}_{z} for various values of χ\chi. When χ=χ~=256\chi=\tilde{\chi}=256, the only error in the distribution is sampling error. We compare this with QPU samples in Fig. S18B, noting, as in the main text, that results look roughly equivalent in quality to MPS at χ=64\chi=64.

To provide a more precise estimate of QPU-equivalent bond dimension, we first define χQ′\chi^{\prime}_{Q} as the intersection in infidelity 1−ℱ1-\mathcal{F} with the interpolating function of many evaluated bond dimensions—this is exactly how we define χQ\chi_{Q}, based on correlation error. This infidelity is a function of the sample-set size used, since we use an empirical estimate to the distribution pp based on sampling. We can suppress the effect of finite sample sizes by extrapolating infidelity to the infinite-sample limit; assuming that sampling error decreases as the square root of the number of samples is sufficient in lower-entropy use cases. Using the infinite-sample limit gives another measure, χQ′′\chi^{\prime\prime}_{Q}, which we analyze instead of χQ′\chi^{\prime}_{Q}. Sampling error in measurement of χQ′\chi^{\prime}_{Q} for one input is shown in Fig. S18D.

We compare χQ\chi_{Q} with χQ′′\chi^{\prime\prime}_{Q} in Fig. S19, for ensembles of 2D problems. As previously noted, sampling error in estimating ℱ\mathcal{F} is severe for distributions with high entropy (i.e., larger problems and faster anneals), which will affect not only direct estimates of χQ′\chi^{\prime}_{Q}, but also extrapolations for χQ′′\chi^{\prime\prime}_{Q}. As seen in Fig. S18D, we can expect small sample sizes to result in underestimates of χQ′′\chi^{\prime\prime}_{Q}, and therefore we should see a deviation downwards—compared to χQ\chi_{Q}—for larger problems and faster anneals. Indeed, in Fig. S19 this is what we see, with strong quantitative agreement between χQ\chi_{Q} and χQ′′\chi^{\prime\prime}_{Q} beginning to decay for larger problems at ta=7 nst_{a}=$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$. Nonetheless, these results give confidence that χQ\chi_{Q}—derived from pairwise correlation errors—is closely linked to the more expressive fidelity measure, and thus the low distributional distance seen for the QPU is not just limited to a plurality of two-body correlations, but rather is based on accurate reproduction of the amplitudes in the final wave function.

V Dynamics of entanglement entropy

The dynamics of entanglement in a quantum quench have been widely studied in quantum many-body systems, both in the context of instantaneous quench and in the context, relevant to this work, of a continuous quench across a QPT116, 112, 31, 117. In “anneal” quenches, the state of an NN-qubit system, prepared initially in the ground state, is evolved in time with slowly varying time-dependent Hamiltonian parameters. In such a finite system, the evolution across a continuous critical point can remain adiabatic for sufficiently slow quenches due to a finite-size gap at the critical point. Consequently, at least in one dimension the entanglement entropy of bipartition follows instantaneous ground-state behavior in this scenario. With faster parameter variation, the system gets excited upon crossing the critical point. Entanglement dynamics in such a case has been studied in a homogeneous 1D TFIM in Refs. 112, 31, showing that at the end of the anneal it grows logarithmically as a function of annealing time tat_{a}, S⁡(t=ta)∝log⁡(ta)S(t=t_{a})\propto\log(t_{a}). Focusing on a finite system 31, there is a crossover between those two regimes, where, in the adiabatic regime, the entanglement entropy at the critical point is S∝log⁡(N)S\propto\log(N) 118. Much less is known about entanglement scaling as a function of number of qubits and quench time tat_{a} in anneal quenches in dimensions d>1d>1.

Accordingly, this work relies mostly on MPS to reveal the scaling behavior of entanglement entropy in anneal quenches for lattice topologies with dimensions d>1d>1. Section VI analyzes the behavior of the QPU-equivalent bond dimension, χQ\chi_{Q}, in terms of the correlation error, ϵc\epsilon_{c}, and ground-truth bond dimension. We further show how we extrapolated our MPS results in bond dimension in order to to establish the ground truths.

VI Comparing and evaluating QPU and MPS experiments

In our experiments, we estimate bipartite von Neumann entanglement entropy SAS_{A} using MPS, with our main practical constraint being the exponential growth of χQ\chi_{Q} as a function of MPS area. The main quantity of interest is the peak entanglement SmaxS_{\text{max}}, which is the maximum both over MPS cuts (A,B)(A,B) and over annealing parameter s=t/tas=t/t_{a}.

VI.1 Estimating entanglement entropy

For both Sm​a​xS_{max} and χQ\chi_{Q}, our approach is to grow χ\chi in factors of 2\sqrt{2} until quantities are converged. Fig. S20 shows convergence of SmaxS_{\text{max}} as a function of MPS bond dimension χ\chi for 2D models with ta=7 nst_{a}=$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ and ta=20 nst_{a}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$. In general we find that SmaxS_{\text{max}} converges to the χ→∞\chi\rightarrow\infty limit faster than χQ\chi_{Q} does.

VI.2 Evaluating ground-truth convergence

The ground truth is ideally obtained in our experiment by taking the limit χ→∞\chi\rightarrow\infty in our MPS simulations. Our distribution accuracy measures—ϵc\epsilon_{c}, ℱ\mathcal{F}, and χQ\chi_{Q}—can be shown to converge as a function of increasing χ\chi approaching this limit much in the same way as entanglement entropy (see Fig. S21).

Statistics converge smoothly to an asymptote as shown, consistent with an exponential tail of truncated singular values 59. Ideally we might observe a clear and sustained asymptote across a large range of χ\chi, indicating that singular value truncation is a negligible source of error. For the hardest problems, this is not practical due to constraints on computational resources. We therefore consider the possibility of extending the reach of MPS simulations by extrapolating in χ\chi.

VI.3 Extrapolation of bond dimension

Since observables in MPS simulations converge as a function of χ\chi, it is often helpful to extrapolate to the limit of unbounded bond dimension (χ=∞\chi=\infty). In this work, we study problems that are near the edge of our computational capacity; we are therefore sufficiently far from convergence that extrapolation must be approached carefully. Extrapolating using too-small bond dimensions is unreliable, so we restrict extrapolation to linear extrapolation of spin-spin correlations in 1/χ1/\chi based on the largest two bond dimensions available. With this restriction, extrapolation to χ=∞\chi=\infty (“full extrapolation”) tends to increase errors, but we find that extrapolating from χmax/2\chi_{\text{max}}/\sqrt{2} and χmax\chi_{\text{max}} to 2​χmax\sqrt{2}\chi_{\text{max}} (“partial extrapolation”) generally reduces errors, particularly in the important region ϵc≈0.03\epsilon_{c}\approx 0.03, where errors are the same order of magnitude as QA errors. Fig. S22 shows examples of 2D, 3D, and biclique ensemble errors for no extrapolation, full extrapolation, and partial extrapolation. Errors are evaluated against the ground truth of maximum available bond dimension χmax\chi_{\text{max}} with no extrapolation. In all cases, partial extrapolation gains at best a factor 2\sqrt{2} in bond dimension. For this reason, although partial extrapolation is useful for refining ground-truth statistical estimates, it does not change the competitiveness of approximate MPS methods; we therefore restrict the use of extrapolation to ground-truth estimation.

VI.4 Effects of time step and stopping point

The main parameter we have tuned to trade speed against accuracy in MPS methods is χ\chi. We found MPS incapable of matching QPU quality for the largest simulations due to both time and memory requirements, and showed that nearly all entanglement entropy must be captured in the MPS to match QPU quality. In Fig. S23A we show that the time evolution of the quench cannot be truncated early—before nearly full entanglement is reached, requiring explosion of the bond dimension—without increasing correlation errors above QPU levels. Therefore some time can be saved by stopping the simulation early, sometimes at a small cost to accuracy, but it will not be useful in reducing memory requirements. Fig. S23B shows entanglement dynamics for a single MPS cut in a single instance as a function of ss. Oscillations in SS after the critical point are hidden when taking the ensemble average and maximum over all cuts.

Throughout the work we have generally used d​t=0.01 nsdt=$0.01\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$; in Fig. S24 we verify that this time step is not a leading source of error.

VI.5 Oblong 2D lattices

We are interested in the scaling of QPU error and entanglement as a function of system size, but for the ensembles studied in the main text, this quickly becomes intractable. One compromise is to study quasi-1D models, which should have favorable scaling in MPS bond dimension requirements. Here we provide data on 6×Ly6{\times}L_{y} cylinders for 6≤Ly≤156\leq L_{y}\leq 15, whose MPS area remains constant at 66.

As in the main text, we once again see flat scaling of QPU error ϵc\epsilon_{c} as a function of system size (Fig. S25A); the bounded MPS width allows extending to larger systems than before. As expected, QPU-equivalent bond dimension χQ\chi_{Q} remains almost constant, with a mild scaling evident at ta=20 nst_{a}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$. In all other systems we saw χQ\chi_{Q} (and SmaxS_{\text{max}}) decreasing as a function of tat_{a}, suggesting that we are near the adiabatic, finite-size regime, as opposed to a large-system Kibble-Zurek regime. The data in Fig. S25B hint that we may see a crossover for larger systems, as was previously observed in 1D chains 31.

VI.6 Area-law scaling for slower quenches

Fig. S26 shows data analogous to Fig. 4 for ta=20 nst_{a}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ instead of 7 ns7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}. We note that correlation errors ϵc\epsilon_{c} are slightly higher for all topologies, and show less size-dependent growth for biclique problems than at 7 ns7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}. In all topologies the longer quenches have lower χQ\chi_{Q}, which allows us to evaluate larger lattices in some cases.

VII Neural networks

Neural network quantum states (NQS) offer a powerful approach to constructing computationally efficient ansätze wave functions. Several types of neural networks, such as complex restricted Boltzmann machines (cRBMs) 47, 119, feed-forward neural networks (FNNs)120, 121, 122, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) 123, 124, 125, 126, and transformers 127, 128, 129, have been employed to approximate ground states and out-of-equilibrium dynamics of quantum many-body systems. For the ground-state problem, the variational Monte Carlo method 130 provides a numerical method for ground-state estimation that is competitive with other state-of-the-art approaches such as tensor networks or quantum Monte Carlo 131. Crucial for the success of this method is the ability to sample from the NQS. Whereas cRBMs and FNNs parameterize unnormalized quantum states and are sampled using Markov chain Monte Carlo, autoregressive models such as RNNs and transformers can be sampled using direct sampling. The latter come with a drawback, since recent results indicate that the autoregressive property of the models may restrict the expressiveness of the model 126, 132.

Beyond ground states, it is possible to simulate the Schrödinger equation on the variational manifold induced by the neural network ansatz. There are currently two approaches to simulate real-time dynamics. The first method is called time-dependent variational Monte Carlo (tVMC) 55. For an NQS |ψθt⟩\ket{\psi_{\theta_{t}}} with pp parameters θ\theta, we calculate the force vector FF at time tt, which depends on the variational energy of the Hamiltonian driving the dynamics. The parameter update to the network for a small time step is then given by

θ˙=S−1​F,\displaystyle\dot{\theta}=S^{-1}F, (S5)

which is closely related to the second-order optimization method of natural gradient descent 133. Here, SS is the metric on the variational manifold induced by the Fubini-Study metric, which is the natural metric on a Hilbert space 134. As SS is a p×pp{\times}p matrix, its inversion takes time O⁡(p3)O(p^{3}), which significantly limits the number of variational parameters that can be used. In addition, both SS and FF must be accurately estimated by sampling from the variational state. For a stable simulation, one typically requires Ns∼104N_{\mathrm{s}}\sim 10^{4} samples per time step. In practice, the matrix SS is typically ill-conditioned and needs to be regularized, for which there exist several approaches 47, 56, 121. The stability of the regularization depends on many factors, including the model architecture, the current variational state and the Hamiltonian. Regularization problems are particularly acute for the RNN architecture. The authors of Ref. 57 argue that RNNs fail for tVMC due to problems with regularizing the SS matrix and recent results indicate that the autoregressive property of the model may restrict its expressiveness 132. Once the SS matrix is successfully regularized, we can solve the differential equation in Eq. S5 for a small time step τ\tau with a second-order differential-equation solver (e.g., Heun’s method or Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg 135).

The second approach for time evolution of variational quantum states is to learn the effect of the time-evolution propagator 𝒰\mathcal{U} on our variational state 136, 56, 137, 57, 138. We refer to this method as projected time-dependent variational Monte Carlo (ptVMC). Here, instead of solving a differential equation at each time step, we explicitly minimize the distance, or infidelity, between the variational state at time tt and time t+τt+\tau:

minθt+τ⁡d⁡(|ψθt+τ⟩,ei​τ​H​|ψθt⟩).\displaystyle\min_{\theta_{t+\tau}}d(\ket{\psi_{\theta_{t+\tau}}},e^{i\tau H}\ket{\psi_{\theta_{t}}}). (S6)

We see that there are two variational states: the state ψθt\psi_{\theta_{t}} at time tt and the state ψθt+τ\psi_{\theta_{t+\tau}}. We “freeze” the parameters θt\theta_{t} and optimize the parameters θt+τ\theta_{t+\tau}. Since ei​τ​He^{i\tau H} is not a local operator that we can easily evaluate on our variational wave function, in practice we have to approximate the full unitary propagator, which can be done in several ways 137, 57, 138. In order to efficiently estimate the infidelity, the authors of Ref. 138 propose a control-variate method to reduce the variance of the estimator similar to Ref. 123. This estimator is quite efficient and, in our experiments, requires only order Ns=102N_{\mathrm{s}}=10^{2} samples per optimization step. However, this comes at the cost of having to minimize the above distance, which could take on the order of 10310^{3} steps in our experiments. Additionally, to achieve stable results at long times, a second-order approximation to the unitary propagator is required, which results in a quadratic increase in complexity that becomes prohibitive at larger system size. In ptVMC, we have traded the sampling problem of tVMC for an optimization problem. The advantage of ptVMC over tVMC is that the former is unconstrained in terms of parameters, which opens up the possibility of using highly expressive models for the simulation of real-time quantum dynamics.

For the problem at hand, which is the simulation of non-adiabatic critical dynamics of the TFIM, the Kibble-Zurek mechanism has been studied with an NQS approach that uses tVMC 48. Additionally, Ref. 57 studied critical dynamics with ptVMC. There are two major differences between previous investigations of critical dynamics and the work presented here. First, the Ising model considered has no symmetries (apart from ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}), hence we cannot make use of translation or lattice symmetries, and we have to use a general variational ansatz. Second, the time scales considered here are beyond what has previously been investigated in the literature. In both Ref. 48 and Ref. 57, NQS approaches are only used close to the critical point. In particular, Ref. 48 notes the NQS method was not stable in the ferromagnetic regime at long times. Finally, a recent work on the simulation of Rydberg arrays was unable to achieve stable results with NQS 4.

We note that before we start the dynamics, the state of the neural network is brought to the ground state of ℋ⁡(0)\mathcal{H}(0) via variational Monte Carlo 130, which converges rapidly to the desired paramagnetic state. In our simulations, we consider only the high-precision square lattices (see Section II). Once the ground state is found, we can attempt to simulate the dynamics with either tVMC or ptVMC. With tVMC, we have been able to simulate systems up to 8×88{\times}8 at a time scale of 7 ns7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} at significant computational cost (3-4 days of compute time with multiple Nvidia T4 GPUs per instance). We chose a fixed time step of τ=10−2\tau=10^{-2} in units of Γc⋅π\Gamma_{c}\cdot\pi (∼4.32 ps\sim$4.32\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{s}$), where Γc\Gamma_{c} is set to the point in the schedule where Γ⁡(s)=𝒥⁡(s)\Gamma(s)=\mathcal{J}(s), which is where the dynamics are critical. Going beyond 8×88{\times}8 is possible for shorter annealing times ta<7 nst_{a}<$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ but would require a large number of GPUs to obtain the necessary samples in a reasonable time. We experimented with adaptive Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg schemes to adaptively set the time step τ\tau. This could significantly reduce the computational cost, since we could speed up the integration at the beginning and slow down as we cross the critical point. However, we were not able to reach stable results for large system sizes with such an approach. The most successful architecture was a cRBM model with the number of hidden units equal to the number of spins (see Figure S28). Due to the O⁡(p3)O(p^{3}) complexity of inverting SS, we limited the number of hidden units to NN (α=1\alpha=1), which was sufficient for the system sizes considered here.

While a Jastrow ansatz 130 proved to be much more numerically stable than the cRBM, it was not expressive enough to capture the dynamics of the system, resulting in larger errors than the cRBM. Feed-forward neural networks with multiple layers showed promise for small system sizes (L<5L<5), but failed at larger system sizes. Similarly, convolutional neural networks were ineffective, most likely due to the lack of translational symmetry of the spin-glass Hamiltonian considered here. Autoregressive architectures like the RNN and transformers came with SS-matrix spectra that were hard to regularize, which resulted in the wrong dynamics.

The main bottleneck in the simulation of the dynamics is the estimation of the SS matrix in Eq. S5. Here, we used a Metropolis-Hasting sampling method with local updates for the Markov chain, which can be parallelized over multiple GPU machines via Message Passing Interface (MPI). As we cross the critical point, the sampling becomes very challenging due to the glassy nature of the system (see Figure S27). The long auto-correlation times result in an increase in variance of the estimators of the forces and SS matrix, necessitating a larger sampling budget to keep errors under control. For regularization of the SS matrix, we explored both the method by Schmitt et al. 121 and Medvidović 56, and found that the latter was the most stable at rcond=10−5r_{\mathrm{cond}}=10^{-5}.

Autoregressive models such as the RNN and transformer fail for tVMC. Attempts to perform dynamics with these models with ptVMC indicate that this method has large (but practically feasible) costs, since the number of steps required to minimize the infidelity for each τ\tau can be of order 10310^{3}. However, a major difficulty with this approach is that the infidelity optimization of Equation S6 can fail to converge, which leads to numerical instabilities. As a result of these convergence issues, we were not able to simulate system sizes larger than L=5L=5. Experiments with the cRBM using ptVMC were much more stable, but not competitive with the tVMC simulations in terms of accuracy, especially at larger system sizes.

Our studies have been limited to square lattices at limited space and quench times; square lattice experiments at 20 ns20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} proved too costly to simulate. If we assume that simulation costs scale up as a function of the correlated volume (consistent with square lattice data from 1 ns1\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} to 7 ns7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} in Figure S28), an NQS approach to more-connected topologies on experimental time scales may exhaust GPU resources at even shorter time scales. All numerical simulations were performed with NetKet 141, a Python framework built on top of JAX 142.

VIII Classical compute resources

This work includes experiments run on a heterogeneous collection of classical CPU and GPU compute resources. These include the Summit and Frontier supercomputers at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, as well as clusters at the Vector Institute, University of British Columbia, Jagiellonian University, and D-Wave.

The main MPS experiments were run on Summit and Frontier, whose workhorse GPUs are, respectively, Nvidia Tesla V100 and AMD Radeon Instinct MI250X. The NQS experiments were performed on multiple Nvidia T4 cards.

Our extrapolation of compute resources is based on measurements from Summit for a 54-qubit system, estimated to require 12 GB12\text{\,}\mathrm{G}\mathrm{B} of memory and 7×1047\text{\times}{10}^{4} seconds at a bond dimension χ=724\chi=724 and ta=7 nst_{a}=$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$. These figures are extrapolated to larger systems and bond dimensions with the leading scaling forms

memory∝N​χ2\text{memory}\propto N\chi^{2} (S7)

and

time∝N​ta​χ3.\text{time}\propto Nt_{a}\chi^{3}. (S8)

since we use a constant time step d​t=0.01 nsdt=$0.01\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ throughout (see Fig. S24).

The V100 GPUs advertise 14 teraFLOPS in single precision; we compare this with a peak performance of 1.7 exaFLOPS for Frontier to produce the comparison in Fig. 5D stating that matching QPU quality on the largest systems would exceed millions of years using all of Frontier.

This is of course an oversimplification in many respects, most importantly ignoring the practical constraints on such computations, which are far too large to perform naively on a GPU. Each Frontier compute node has 4 TB4\text{\,}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{B} of memory, and the total storage is 700 PB700\text{\,}\mathrm{P}\mathrm{B}. These figures are marked in Fig. S29. We note that the largest bond dimension simulated to date81 is 216=6.5×1042^{16}=$6.5\text{\times}{10}^{4}$.

IX Critical exponents and dynamic finite-size scaling ansatz

In this section we briefly explain the dynamic finite-size scaling analysis of Fig. 5B, which generalizes the approach of Ref. 25 from cubic to multiple topologies.

A crucial element of any claim of beyond-classical performance is evidence that experimental results scale correctly beyond the classically verifiable regime. Since we simulate traversals of quantum phase transitions (QPTs), we can appeal to the existing theoretical foundation of critical phenomena to provide this evidence. For large problems, i.e., in the thermodynamic limit, the Kibble-Zurek mechanism 28, 143, 144, 32, 33, 34 allows us to predict the scaling of correlations and related quantities—including the Binder cumulant—as a function of quench time. More specifically, quantities will be related by the universal critical exponents reflecting the universality class of the QPT. This approach has previously been used to compare quantum simulations with theoretical expectations in superconducting quantum annealers145, 24, 23, 25 and annealed Rydberg arrays26, 58.

Fig. 5B shows data collapses for the Binder cumulant

U=12​(3−[⟨q4⟩][⟨q2⟩]2),U=\frac{1}{2}\left(3-\frac{[\langle q^{4}\rangle]}{[\langle q^{2}\rangle]^{2}}\right), (S9)

where [⋅][\cdot] indicates an average over disorder realizations. The Binder cumulant gives a statistical signature of phase transitions. In this work, we use UU to estimate—via collapse—the Kibble-Zurek exponent

μ=z+1/ν,\mu=z+1/\nu, (S10)

where zz and ν\nu are the dynamic exponent and the equilibrium correlation-length exponent pertaining to the QPT at hand29. That is, the paramagnetic-to-spin-glass QPT in the universality class for each topology. These are 2D Ising, 3D Ising, 3D Ising, 3D Ising, and mean-field (fully connected) for square, cubic, cubic no-dimer, diamond, and biclique, respectively.

At the critical point in the quench, it is expected60 that both ⟨q2⟩\langle q^{2}\rangle and UU should collapse (separately) as a functions of LL and tat_{a}. While ⟨q2⟩\langle q^{2}\rangle is less statistically sensitive, collapse of UU is preferable here for two reasons. First, ⟨q2⟩\langle q^{2}\rangle was found25 to be susceptible to distortion from post-critical dynamics between the QPT and the end of the quench, where the output state is read. Second, ⟨q2⟩\langle q^{2}\rangle must be collapsed as a function of both μ\mu and the anomalous dimension η\eta; the collapse of UU is only in one parameter μ\mu, making the fit more straightforward in the face of limited system sizes and uncertainty in η\eta.

Thus we measure UU for multiple linear system sizes LL and quench times tat_{a}. For each topology (and treating high-precision and low-precision ensembles separately), we expect data collapse when plotting UU against ta​L−μt_{a}L^{-\mu}. We therefore minimize deviation between the collapsed data and a common collapse curve of the parametric form

f⁡(x)=a0+a1​log⁡(1+exp⁡(a2​(x−a3)))f(x)=a_{0}+a_{1}\log{(1+\exp{(a_{2}(x-a_{3})}))} (S11)

in the (log⁡(U)\log{(U)}, log⁡(ta​L−μ)\log{(t_{a}L^{-\mu})}) plane (as in Ref. 25, Fig. 3c–d), where for bicliques we take L=M1/8=(N/4)1/8L=M^{1/8}=(N/4)^{1/8} based on the upper-critical dimension 8 (Ref. 62). Estimates of μ\mu can be impacted by the effect of small inputs in the best-fit collapse; we therefore estimate μ\mu using the three largest simulated sizes of each topology, as well as estimating using all sizes. The results, along with related literature values, are summarized in Table 2.

Precise estimates of UU require averaging over many spin-glass realizations (often called “samples” in the spin-glass community). Therefore instead of focusing on 20-instance ensembles, which allow us to keep classical compute resources within reason, we simulate many realizations. For each of 300 QPU calls, we generate a distinct random realization for each individual parallel embedding into the qubit lattice. Thus the number of spin-glass instances simulated in QA for this analysis ranges from 300 (for the largest square and cubic instances) to 20,400 (for the smallest instances, where many random realizations are run in parallel in each QPU call).

Previous studies have provided independent estimates of zz and 1/ν1/\nu, allowing us to validate the scaling of correlations in the system beyond the classically verifiable regime. We compare our experimental estimates of μ\mu against the results of classical Monte Carlo simulations (for square and cubic) and mean-field theory (for biclique).

For 2D and 3D, there has been some controversy over whether or not zz is finite. For 2D, this was settled very recently37 through the consideration of distinct parity sectors in the state space, using MC simulations of low-precision L×LL{\times}L square lattices (with fully periodic boundaries) with LL ranging from 88 to 2424. The authors extracted distinct estimates for the finite-size measurement (fixing their fitting parameter ηe0=0\eta_{e}^{0}=0) and the large-system limit of, respectively,

μ=z+1/ν=1.7​(2)+0.9​(1)=2.6​(3)\mu=z+1/\nu=1.7(2)+0.9(1)=2.6(3) (S12)

and

μ=z+1/ν=2.46​(17)+0.71​(24)=3.27​(41),\mu=z+1/\nu=2.46(17)+0.71(24)=3.27(41), (S13)

both of which are in remarkably good agreement with our all-size and largest-size estimates of μ\mu from low-precision glasses (2.67​(30)2.67(30) and 2.99​(19)2.99(19) respectively). Future experiments in a larger QPU might clarify finite-size effects in these estimates. The classical estimates of Ref. 37 updated the previous literature estimates146 of z=1.50​(5)z=1.50(5) and ν=1.0​(1)\nu=1.0(1)—which are by now outdated in terms of computational reach—with extensive state-of-the-art GPU simulations. When considering small-system effects, the three estimates of μ\mu (2.6​(3)2.6(3), 2.5​(2)2.5(2) and 2.67​(30)2.67(30) from, respectively, Ref. 37, Ref. 146, and this work) concur extremely well.

For 3D, the finite-zz scenario is supported by considerable evidence, including the above result for 2D and large-scale experiments in quantum annealers (this work itself and Ref. 25), and we may reasonably take the position that zz is indeed finite. The prevailing classical estimate of z=1.3z=1.3 is, like the previous 2D estimate146, computationally outdated and could benefit from an extension of the methods and computational resources brought to bear in Ref. 37. The estimate of 1/ν=1.55​(11)1/\nu=1.55(11) has recently been updated for the purposes of evaluating QA25. Our estimates of μ\mu, summarized as μ=2.72​(16)\mu=2.72(16), are again in line with previous estimates. The fact that this estimate is slightly lower than that reported by Ref. 25 may be due to reduced noise in the ADV2 processor as compared to the ADV1 processor used previously, with possible influence of smaller system sizes used in the collapse in this work.

For biclique, we expect behavior in line with mean-field critical exponents z=2z=2 and 1/ν=41/\nu=4, which would mean a collapse upon rescaling tat_{a} by M−μ/8≈M−3/4M^{-\mu/8}\approx M^{-3/4} (Ref. 62). There are large per-size fluctuations relative to the other topologies; this may be related to per-size configurations of inter-dimer coupling structure. The estimates based on M=8M=8 to 2424 are nonetheless very close to mean-field expectations of an infinite-dimensional topology.

In addition to the problem classes considered in the main text, we apply the same analysis to cubic no-dimer lattices, with collapses shown in Fig. S30 and compared with diamond lattices. We expect both of these to exhibit behavior consistent with the 3D quantum Ising spin glass universality class. For cubic no-dimer, we consider the same problem sizes as for cubic dimer. Both cubic no-dimer and diamond inputs admit estimates of μ\mu consistent with the 3D quantum Ising spin-glass universality class, as summarized in Table 3. The slightly higher estimate compared to cubic dimer—while still within uncertainties—may be related to the larger effective system sizes.

For 1D systems, we estimate μ\mu by measuring kink density n¯\bar{n} as a function of tat_{a} for a large system (L=512L=512, Fig. S31). As in previous works 24, 26, the measured scaling exponent is consistent with the expected KZ defect scaling n¯∝ta−1/μ\bar{n}\propto t_{a}^{-1/\mu} with z=1z=1 and ν=1\nu=1.

Taken as a whole, the agreement in critical scaling, which relates time and correlation length via the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, provides indirect validation of QA results beyond the classically simulable regime. This provides a complement to the precise quantitative agreement shown for small problems.

X Monte Carlo dynamics

Tensor-network approaches provide faithful approximations to quantum dynamics, and generate accurate sample distributions in the appropriate parametric limits. There are other methods, especially various Monte Carlo (MC) dynamics, which have been proposed to mimic the output of quantum annealers. Here we discuss several such MC dynamics and show that they cannot emulate coherent out-of-equilibrium quantum dynamics. The dynamics we discuss here are simulated annealing (SA)147, simulated quantum annealing (SQA) with path-integral Monte Carlo148, 149, spin-vector MC (SVMC)150, 151, and SVMC with transverse-field freeze-out (SVMC-TF)152.

On one hand, these methods are computationally inexpensive compared to tensor-network approaches, and therefore can be run on all system sizes used in our QA experiments. On the other hand, they have already been shown to fail various emulation tests in toy problems153, 154. In particular, all of these dynamics fail in one way or another to qualitatively reproduce quantum dynamics even in a pure one-dimensional system 24 (see SM for Ref. 24, Figs. S4 and S5).

Since these methods can be run at large scale, we can collapse the Binder cumulant for these dynamics, as in Fig. 5B, and compare against quantum mechanical values. This was already done in Ref. 25, which showed clearly distinct Kibble-Zurek exponents for QA, SQA, and SA in (dimerized) cubic problems. As a consequence, QA was shown to have a dynamical advantage in optimization for these spin glasses. We now repeat a similar test for SVMC and SVMC-TF to further solidify the deviation between these classical dynamics and the Schrödinger dynamics realized within QA. For SA we use a geometric cooling schedule as in Ref. 25. For SVMC and SVMC-TF we use the model quench schedule with a low temperature equal to Γ⁡(s∗)/64\Gamma(s^{*})/64, where s∗s* is the crossing point with Γ⁡(s∗)=𝒥⁡(s∗)\Gamma(s^{*})=\mathcal{J}(s^{*}). SA is run up to ta=215t_{a}=2^{15} Monte Carlo sweeps, and SVMC and SVMC-TF are run up to 2172^{17} Monte Carlo sweeps. For such slow anneals we do not expect sensitivity to the shape of the annealing schedule.

Results are shown in Fig. S32 for SA, SVMC, and SVMC-TF for high-precision problems only. SQA is far slower, so we disregard it since its consistency with quantum quench dynamics has already been refuted in 1D and 3D systems. For the three dynamics, we find consistent Binder cumulant estimates that are much higher than quantum values.

XI Spatial decomposition techniques

Experimental evidence and theory presented throughout the paper are consistent with the notion that in some of our experimental systems the correlation length, ξ\xiVIIVII VII As discussed elsewhere, a correlation length scale might originate in the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, we call the Kibble Zurek correlation length ξ^\hat{\xi}. For purposes of this section we need not assume the Kibble-Zurek mechanism to be the source of correlations, or assume a scaling form., is not system spanning, particularly in higher precision (lower-energy scale) models at shorter time scales, and in lower dimensions. Intuition suggests that correlation length, more than system size, should dictate the complexity of approximate simulation. In other words, we must consider the possibility that locality can be exploited through spatial decomposition of the simulation task.

This is natively in our PEPS methods, which, as a result, find success in square lattice models on short time scales. PEPS provides a globally consistent ansatz for the quantum state. Given efficient contraction, this allows for estimation of both local and global observables. For calculation of local observables, some neighborhood contraction (proportional to ξ\xi) is expected to be sufficient.

For the purposes of estimating local observables, even simpler approximations than neighborhood-limited PEPS contraction may suffice. If correlation length ξ\xi is short throughout some dynamical process, we might truncate the system to a cluster of scale proportional to ξ\xi and only simulate dynamics on such a cluster, with statistics at its center well approximated. Unlike a PEPS neighborhood contraction, there needn’t be an approximation of quantum phenomena beyond the cluster boundary, or at the boundary (in the following we assume that the clusters have open boundary conditions). Such subsystems might be simulated with an MPS or PEPS method, or by the QPU itself. In the context of MPS, the complexity of simulation can then be reduced in proportion to the area-law of the cluster with the error being controlled by a reduced bond dimension due to the smaller cluster size. In the context of the QPU, we might aim to estimate statistics associated with systems that are beyond a programmable scale. Such a “cluster approximation” has the benefit of being much simpler than PEPS.

In both QPU and MPS cases, we might simulate many clusters centered at various points on a lattice, and then estimate correlations in the interior of such clusters. We study this for MPS sampling in XI.1 and for QPU subsampling in sections XI.1 and XI.2. In Section XI.3 we consider a simple extrapolation method, based on such statistics, that allows accurate estimates of global statistics in some circumstances.

XI.1 Cluster approximations with MPS

We already showed in the main text (Figs. 2 and 4) that the bond dimension required for MPS simulations to achieve the QPU accuracy follows area-law growth. Hence, naively it is expected that with increasing number of qubits the cost of MPS simulations attaining QPU accuracy should eventually go beyond the capability of classical computational resources. In this section we use MPS simulations on multiple open-boundary clusters around a chosen site inside an Lx×LyL_{x}{\times}L_{y} square lattice cylinder, periodic in yy, at a scale Lx=Ly=8L_{x}=L_{y}=8; see Fig.S33A. Panels B (ta=7 nst_{a}=$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$) and C (ta=20 nst_{a}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$) compare a subset of ground-truth spin-spin correlation estimates against those obtained with square clusters of sizes Lc×LcL_{c}{\times}L_{c} with Lc=4,5,6L_{c}=4,5,6. For ta=7 nst_{a}=$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$, increasing accuracy is apparent as LcL_{c} grows, with a good quantitative match in the majority of nearest and next-nearest neighbor correlations already at Lc=5L_{c}=5. Accuracy is reduced as tat_{a} increases towards 20 ns20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} (Fig. S33C). This gives a qualitative understanding that for higher tat_{a} we need larger clusters to reproduce accurate short-range correlations, in line with increasing correlation lengths.

The cluster position on the full lattice can be displaced to attain all short-range correlations. The quantum dynamics of all these small clusters can be trivially parallelized leading to only linear growth in the numerical cost with the system size (NN for square clusters, LL for boundary-spanning stripe clusters). A similar technique has been used extensively for performing Monte Carlo simulations on quantum-classical hybrid models 155 under the name of traveling cluster approximation (TCA). We study the accuracy of TCA for quantum annealing by calculating ϵc\epsilon_{c} attained by the TCA against MPS simulation of the full system (Fig. S34). We tried three different cluster shapes: square clusters (Lc×LcL_{c}{\times}L_{c}), open stripes (Lc×LyL_{c}{\times}L_{y}), and periodic stripes (Lx×LcL_{x}{\times}L_{c}). We noticed all three cases perform well for small tat_{a}. For example, for ta=0.3 nst_{a}=$0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$, all three TCAs for the 6×66\times 6 system with cluster of linear length 44 give QPU-level accuracy, and the clusters of length 55 can produce trustworthy results up to ta=2 nst_{a}=$2\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$. The correlation error grows as we increase tat_{a}. This is expected because the correlation length increases with tat_{a} and the longer-range correlations, inaccessible to the small cluster, also becomes relevant. We also found periodic stripes perform best, followed by the open stripes and then square clusters. However, even at equivalent size, the cost of simulation of obtaining high accuracy results is a non-trivial function of the topology that must be considered. Periodic stripes require support for boundary spanning entanglement that must be accommodated with higher bond dimension. Similarly, the open stripes are costlier than square clusters of equivalent width not only in proportion to their additional length, but due to the higher bond dimension required to accommodate higher entanglement entropy (anticipated logarithmic corrections in the entropy as the system is passing through the QCP in the annealing process).

XI.2 Cluster approximations with the QPU

As shown in the previous section, MPS methods become computationally expensive for large systems because even though correlation lengths are short (for the annealing times of our annealing experiments), they can still encompass many qubits. When MPS simulations become unfeasible, one can then think of using the QPU as a solver for each the traveling cluster. It is therefore possible to use QPU subsampling to explore the relationship between large systems and the larger clusters required for their approximation. Moreover, we can compare the QPU statistics with and without clustering approximations. For small systems, we have established that the cluster scale required for accurate estimation in this context is a good proxy for the cluster scale required for emulation of ground-truth statistics.

In this section we show that clustered approximations at these larger scales are indeed sufficient when the cluster volume is large compared to cluster-boundary, and when the correlation length (controlled primarily by annealing time tat_{a}) is relatively small. In some scenarios we show that even clusters at a scale comparable to the full system are insufficient for estimation of local correlations, indicating the presence of significant system-spanning correlations.

XI.2.1 Two dimensions

For large 2D systems of size L×LL{\times}L with one periodic dimension, we use the following spatial decomposition to determine spin-spin correlations:

  • •

    Choose a block width W≤LW\leq L.

  • •

    In the periodic dimension, delete every WWth row of couplers, leaving behind a set of W×LW{\times}L blocks that span from one open boundary to the other. Do this for every possible offset (00 to WW, ignoring divisibility issues which should be handled in the obvious way).

  • •

    Simulate all the W×LW{\times}L blocks and determine spin-spin correlations within the blocks.

  • •

    Combine the correlations. For two spins that are in a block together, we take the weighted average of blocks that maximize the minimum distance of the two spins to the block cuts. Correlations with spins near the block boundaries can be discarded, or not. Long-distance correlations can be inferred from short-ranged correlations, or simply set to zero.

The cluster shapes are shown in S35 for an 18×1818{\times}18 lattice; we might call this approach a rotating-cluster approximation (RCA).

In Fig. S36A–B we show experimental results for L=8L=8 and W=4,8W=4,8, performing cluster simulations and the full-lattice simulation with QPU; at this scale we can compute error against the MPS ground truth (Fig. S36A). For fast quenches (ta<4 nst_{a}<$4\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$) correlations are sufficiently short-ranged that RCA is indistinguishable from the full simulation, even for W=4W=4. As tat_{a} increases to 20 ns20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}, RCA error becomes significantly larger than full-lattice error. Under the simplifying assumption that error from cluster size and QPU-to-model error are independent and add in quadrature for ϵc\epsilon_{c}, the fact that RCA error is larger than 2\sqrt{2} times full-lattice error certifies that an RCA approach (at W=8W=8) cannot produce simulation output with lower error than QA, even if the clusters were simulated exactly.

Fig. S36B represents the same experiments as Fig. S36A, but shows ϵc\epsilon_{c} as calculated against a QPU “ground truth” rather than an MPS ground truth. The full-lattice baseline becomes a measurement of ϵc\epsilon_{c} between two independently-run but otherwise identical QPU experiments, essentially a noise floor that captures QPU device variation and noise as well as statistical noise (sampling error). Here, for short tat_{a}, errors are significantly smaller than in Fig. S36A, suggesting that QPU-to-model error is dominant. However, for longer tat_{a} RCA is almost identical between Fig. S36A and B, indicating that cluster boundary effects become dominant.

We move to larger systems (L=18L=18) in Fig. S36C, for which we were unable to compute a ground truth with MPS. Note when W=18W=18 we are performing 18 times as many simulations on the same number of spins, and combining the correlations determined from all rotations of the single cut. Since we do not have a ground truth for L>8L>8, we instead take our reference distribution (and correlations) from the full-lattice simulation as in Fig. S36B.

As expected, this approach yields correlation errors that decrease as WW increases. We also see that the signal deviates upwards from the noise floor as tat_{a} increases. This is compatible with correlation length growth. The Kibble-Zurek mechanism anticipates a correlation length scaling as ξ^∝ta1/μ\hat{\xi}\propto t_{a}^{1/\mu}, where μ\mu is the Kibble-Zurek exponent. This is loosely corroborated by the fact that we require W≈6W\approx 6 to approach the noise floor at ta=7 nst_{a}=$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$, and W≈9W\approx 9 to approach it at ta=20 nst_{a}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$, given that μ≈3\mu\approx 3 in 2D systems.

These experiments are based on 20 inputs and 50,000 samples each, and the noise floor (solid line with square markers) is much higher than for the smaller system in Fig. S36B: Correlations at large distance (large compared to the correlation length) are noise-dominated, and the number of contributions scales as N2N^{2}. These are integrated with equal weight in the numerator and denominator of ϵc\epsilon_{c}, which is the origin of the sampling error.

What conclusions can we draw from this data? Error appears to be weakly dependent on system size (Figs.4A and S26A), thus we anticipate that QPU-to-model error for L=18L=18 should be close to that for L=8L=8. Observe that W=6W=6 RCA error for ta=20 nst_{a}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ in Fig. S36C is more than twice that of the L=8L=8 full-lattice simulation in Fig. S36A. We take this as evidence that W=6W=6 is insufficient for an RCA approach to match QPU error, even assuming exact simulation of the clusters. Conversely, the fact that L=18L=18, W=9W=9 error in Fig. S36C is slightly less than L=8L=8 QPU-to-model error in Fig. S36A suggests that an RCA approach might achieve comparable ϵc\epsilon_{c} to QPU full-lattice simulation. The scaling of χQ\chi_{Q} for strips of fixed width is anticipated to be at most logarithmic (in strip length), so only modest growth in MPS resources might be required to simulate local correlations accurately for L≳9L\gtrsim 9.

This analysis only applies to ϵc\epsilon_{c}, and does not imply that full-lattice states can be sampled routinely based on cluster output. However, we find this to at least support the possibility that for square lattices with L=18L=18 and ta=20 nst_{a}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$, spin-spin correlations might be spoofed via spatial decomposition.

As already shown in the context of PEPS, square lattice problems are relatively easier than other lattices we simulate. We now use the same RCA approach to establish that for three-dimensional lattices at the maximum experimental scale, such clustering approaches are not successful.

XI.2.2 Three dimensions

One can extend the square lattice approach to three dimensions in a straightforward way, decomposing a 3D system with planar cuts through the periodic dimension just as we decomposed a 2D system with linear cuts through the periodic dimension. Here we do so, first showing results in Fig. S37A for an L×L×LL\times L\times L dimerized cubic system with L=6L=6. As in 2D, we see that deviation from the noise floor increases with tat_{a}. Indeed, it appears possible to spoof correlations fairly accurately with W=4W=4 up to ta=7 nst_{a}=$7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$. However, at 20 ns20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} there is significant deviation even at W=6W=6, where any two spins are inside the bulk of a cluster.

We repeat the approach for cubic no-dimer inputs, which—exactly like the diamond lattice—are four-regular and have girth (shortest cycle) six. As in the cubic dimer case, we see in Fig. S37B a separation for W=L=6W=L=6 at ta=20 nst_{a}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$, although it is less pronounced. For diamond lattices, we apply this approach to the largest defect-free lattice size, and find in Fig. S37C a very strong effect even at W=L=12W=L=12—this is possibly in part due to the nature of the cluster boundary, which sees each spin lose two of four incident couplers, rather than one of four in cubic no-dimer lattices, and one of six neighboring dimers in the dimerized cubic lattice. Unlike in the square lattice case, errors for RCA at ta=20 nst_{a}=$20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}$ are in all cases well above the threshold we anticipate to characterize the QPU.

These results suggest that spoofing results for cubic, cubic no-dimer, and diamond systems by spatial decomposition is unpromising in this parametric regime. The simplest explanation for this is the presence of significant system-spanning correlations, the presence of which place limitations on a variety of related approximation methods.

XI.3 Classical extrapolation of statistics from local to global

Spatial decomposition techniques typically allow estimation of local observables such as correlations and marginal probability distributions. However, inference of global properties is technically challenging on the basis of this information, particularly in the absence of a simple parametric model for the global distribution. In this section, we show that simple heuristics can, in some circumstances, extrapolate from (sufficiently accurate and numerous) local statistics of the projected distribution to macroscopic properties, with some tolerable error. In particular, we demonstrated examples in which fully visible Boltzmann distributions trained on accurate local pairwise correlations can be used to infer long-range correlations and approximately sample full states with an accuracy comparable to the QPU (in sampling a ground truth).

A fully visible classical Boltzmann machine, also called an exponential model, takes the form of P⁡(x)=1Z​exp⁡(θi​fi​(x))P(x)=\frac{1}{Z}\exp(\theta_{i}f_{i}(x)), where ZZ is a normalization constant also called the partition function. The parameterization of this model can be inferred from expectations ⟨fi​(x)⟩\langle f_{i}(x)\rangle. Supposing the statistics are geometrically local (e.g. fi​(x)=xi​xjf_{i}(x)=x_{i}x_{j}, for variables nearby on some lattice), then only local statistics are necessary. For smooth probability distribution described by essentially-classical correlation decay at larger geometric distances, a BM might provide good approximations (provided suitable choices are made for the set fi​(x)f_{i}(x)). Whilst it is technically NP-complete to train from sufficient statistics, training of a lattice model at the scales we present is practically straightforward, and methods such as maximum pseudolikelihood inference offer alternative efficient routes to model inference.

Assuming long-range correlations are weak and well described classically, and that we have access to accurate local observables, then we can train our Boltzmann machine from local observables. A complex pattern of local correlations in the projected distribution, perhaps induced by entanglement, might be reproduced by a sufficiently complex set of fi​(x)f_{i}(x). The full distribution, and statistics thereof, are then smooth extrapolations consistent with the local observables. The Boltzmann distribution can, for practical purposes, be sampled by Markov chain Monte Carlo (short correlation length implies short autocorrelation time) and so we can reproduce any statistic amenable to Monte-Carlo sampling with some systematic error reflecting the restriction in the choice of fif_{i} and quality of the training data.

Sections XI.2.1-XI.1 demonstrate MPS and QPU methods for obtaining local correlation estimates. PEPS methods based on the neighborhood contraction might also provide a basis for extrapolation in principle.

We found in our analysis of L×LL{\times}L square high and low-precision systems up to a scale 8×88{\times}8 that achieving small ϵc\epsilon_{c}, for emulation of either the QPU or ground-truth distribution, was equally challenging (the error threshold obtained in training was similar for a fixed bound on the scale of local observables). Furthermore we were able to establish a strong correlation between ϵc\epsilon_{c}, classical fidelity and other distributional measures—measuring long range correlations as captured by ϵc\epsilon_{c} was established as a good proxy for accurate reproduction of the full distribution. With this assumed, we present an analysis based on accurate estimation of ϵc\epsilon_{c} only. Since observables approximated by large clusters are less expensive to create for QPU distributions, relative to MPS-based data, we present the approximation for the QPU generated approximations (XI.2.1), understanding this to hold qualitatively also for approximation of the ground truth.

Figure S38 shows the result of training an Boltzmann machine to infer all correlations (and state probabilities) from local correlations within some geometrically constrained distance.VIIIVIII VIII Geometric distance being the Euclidean distance in the standard square lattice representation. For geometric distance 3 we include only pairs separated by at most 2 couplers (graph distance 2); in other cases all correlations are included. For the 8×88{\times}8 cylinder, the quality of the QPU distribution is captured by ϵc\epsilon_{c}, measuring the distance from the ground truth to the QPU. For our approximation, we measure the gap between the cluster-based approximation and the QPU (as the ground truth). When the latter error is smaller than the former, our cluster method can be considered to have succeeded in emulating the global distribution. At 7 ns7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} we show that sufficiently accurate calculation of pairwise correlations up to Euclidean distance ≲3\lesssim 3 on square lattice at 8×88{\times}8 scale is sufficient to train a Boltzmann machine with high accuracy. At 20 ns20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}, we do not see such a success, presumably due to longer correlation lengths. We present the training result based on both ideal data (from the full QPU distribution) and the estimates based on the rotating-cluster approximation. When incorporating data from sufficiently large geometric distance we expect the boundary effect to degrade performance of Boltzmann models trained with the latter set of correlations; this is found to be the case. At 7 ns7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} the accuracy of local statistics is excellent, and we see little degradation in the performance out to distance 3. By contrast at 20 ns20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} the correlation estimates are weaker, and we see an immediate deviation between the trained estimates.

As shown in the main text, our distribution can become less entangled at larger tat_{a}, particularly as we cross over to the adiabatic regime with system-spanning correlations. Less-entangled distributions favor this classical approximation method—assuming local observables may be accurately estimated. However, correlation lengths increase with tat_{a}, degrading the quality of local estimates attainable by cluster approximations. The quality of local estimations is also impacted by dimensionality: for fixed correlation length the boundary effect (relative to the cluster bulk) has a more favorable ratio in low dimensions, in addition to the fact that correlation lengths can grow more quickly. In this section we have shown that at 7 ns7\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s}, 2D high-precision spin-glass problems at scale 8×88{\times}8 and larger may be susceptible to clustering approximations, even where global statistics are concerned. For other experimental systems with larger correlation length relative to linear scale (20 ns20\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{s} experiments, lower-precision, and/or higher-dimensional models) the method is understood to fail.
